result.markdown: # Tutorial 1: Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness {#i-ep01 .unnumbered} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 1, you can - fit a simple regression in R and interpret its results with units, - check the assumptions of a model with residual plots and influence measures, - judge a model with its coefficient table, $R^2$, and the F-test, - check an AI reading of a regression output and correct its errors. ::: Tutorials are exam preparation sessions. The tasks below are exam-style questions. You take the exam in TestVision, and R is available. Try each task yourself before you look at the solution. You may use AI for this, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 1 and 2. Lecture 3 is on the day before this tutorial: read its lecture material, and do its practice after the tutorial. Keep the Lectures 1--3 sections of the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) open while you work. If the notation slows you down, review [Mathematics Refresher: straight lines, slopes, and intercepts](../resources/math-refresher.html#straight-lines-slopes-and-intercepts) and [powers, roots, and squared deviations](../resources/math-refresher.html#powers-roots-and-squared-deviations). Write from memory: 1. the simple linear regression model, 2. the fitted line, 3. the residual, 4. the formula for $R^2$, 5. the null hypothesis of the overall F-test. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i$. 2. $\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i$. 3. $e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i$. 4. $R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}=\text{SSR}/\text{SST}$. 5. $H_0:\beta_1=0$ in simple regression (all slopes zero in general). ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial Try each task in R before you open the answer. A complete written answer does five things. It names the sample, shows the calculation, and reports values with units. It interprets the values in context. And it states one important limit of the model or of the data. Tasks 1 to 5 and Task 7 follow one founder question through all steps of Lectures 1 to 3: how closely does the valuation agreed with the sharks follow the valuation that the founder claims? All tasks use the Shark Tank teaching file. The valuations are in millions of dollars: the valuation agreed on air (`agreed_m`) and the valuation claimed by the founder (`claimed_m`). The code below builds the data in the same way as in Lectures 1 to 3. It keeps the deals in which the sharks took a share of the company, and it converts both valuations from dollars to millions of dollars. The eight deals in which the sharks took no share of the company have no agreed valuation (the file records it as zero), so they are left out. The last line prints the number of deals that remain. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 nrow(vals) # deals for a share of the company ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 874 ``` ::: ::: ### Task 1: Fit and interpret (Lecture 1) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Fit the simple regression of the agreed valuation (`agreed_m`) on the claimed valuation (`claimed_m`), among the deals for a share of the company. Then report: 1. the sample, with its number of deals, 2. the fitted equation, 3. the interpretation of the slope with units, in one sentence, 4. the limit of the intercept's meaning, in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Sample: Fitted equation: Interpretation of the slope: Limit of the intercept's meaning: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) coef(val_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) claimed_m -0.06798986 0.64874084 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Sample: the 874 deals for a share of the company. - Fitted equation: $\widehat y = -0.068 + 0.649x$, with both valuations in \$ millions. - Interpretation of the slope: a claimed valuation that is \$1 million higher is associated with an agreed valuation that is on average about \$0.65 million higher, so about two thirds of a higher claim shows up in the agreed valuation. - Limit of the intercept's meaning: a claimed valuation of zero is outside the observed range, so the intercept (about $-\$68{,}000$) has no useful business meaning of its own. ::: ### Task 2: Fitted value and residual (Lecture 1) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the Task 1 model of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation, both in \$ millions. A founder claimed a valuation of \$5 million and the deal was agreed on air at a valuation of \$2.5 million. 1. Calculate the fitted value of this deal. 2. Calculate the residual of this deal. 3. Interpret the sign of the residual in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Fitted value: Residual: Meaning of the sign: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) unname(2.5 - predict(val_model, newdata = data.frame(claimed_m = 5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.6757143 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. It prints the residual. - Fitted value: with $x=5$ (in \$ millions), $\widehat y = -0.068 + 0.649 \times 5 \approx 3.18$, or about \$3.18 million. - Residual: the observed $y = 2.5$, so $e = 2.5 - 3.18 = -0.68$, about $-\$680{,}000$. This is about 21% of the fitted value. - Meaning of the sign: the negative sign means that this deal was agreed below the model's fitted conditional mean for a claimed valuation of \$5 million. ::: ### Task 3: Diagnostics and influence (Lecture 2) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Produce the residual-versus-fitted plot and the normal Q--Q plot for the Task 1 model of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation. 1. Name two problems with the assumptions that you can see in the plots. For each one, say in one sentence what in the plots shows it. 2. Count the standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$ and the observations with a Cook's distance above $4/n$. 3. State the three-step rule for handling a flagged observation. 4. Name one assumption that these plots cannot assess, and say in one sentence what information would assess it. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: First problem, and what in the plots shows it: Second problem, and what in the plots shows it: Number with a standardised residual beyond ±3: Number with a Cook's distance above 4/n: Rule for flagged observations: Assumption the plots cannot assess, and what would assess it: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1) plot(fitted(val_model), residuals(val_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", alpha.f = 0.35), bty = "n", xlab = "Fitted agreed valuation ($ millions)", ylab = "Residual ($ millions)") abline(h = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00") qqnorm(rstandard(val_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#009E73", alpha.f = 0.40), bty = "n", main = "", xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile", ylab = "Standardised residual") qqline(rstandard(val_model), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](t01-exam-prep_files/figure-html/iep01-task3-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(old_par) c(big_rstandard = sum(abs(rstandard(val_model)) > 3), cooks_flagged = sum(cooks.distance(val_model) > 4 / nobs(val_model))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` big_rstandard cooks_flagged 25 64 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - First problem, and what in the plots shows it: the spread of the residuals widens with the fitted value, and this fan shape shows heteroskedasticity, so it challenges homoskedasticity. - Second problem, and what in the plots shows it: the Q--Q plot leaves the line at both ends, with several extreme residuals on both sides, which challenges normality and suggests that some deals may be influential. - Number with a standardised residual beyond ±3: 25 deals, about 3% of the 874. - Number with a Cook's distance above 4/n: 64 deals, about 7% of the 874. - Rule for flagged observations: investigate, report, never silently delete. - Assumption the plots cannot assess, and what would assess it: the plots cannot assess independence. To assess it, you need knowledge of how the data were collected, for example whether the same sharks or founders appear in several rows. ::: ### Task 4: Coefficient inference (Lecture 3) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the coefficient table and the 95% confidence intervals of the Task 1 model of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation. 1. Test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$ in five steps, with the critical value approach at the 5% level. 2. Report the 95% confidence interval for $\beta_1$, verify it by hand from the estimate and the standard error, and compare it with the interval in the output. 3. Would heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors fix both problems with the assumptions that you named in Task 3? Answer yes or no, and explain in one or two sentences. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Test, hypotheses: Test, test statistic: Test, critical value and rejection region: Test, observed value: Test, conclusion: Interval, formula: Interval, given values: Interval, calculations: Interval: Interval, comparison with the output: Robust standard errors, yes or no, and why: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) summary(val_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) -0.06798986 0.06847892 -0.9928582 3.210545e-01 claimed_m 0.64874084 0.01106883 58.6096854 1.099793e-304 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(val_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) -0.2023926 0.06641292 claimed_m 0.6270162 0.67046551 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Test, hypotheses: $H_0:\beta_1=0$, $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. The significance level is 5%. - Test, test statistic: $T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, with $874-2=872$ degrees of freedom. - Test, critical value and rejection region: $t_{0.975,\,872}$ = `qt(0.975, 872)` = 1.963. Reject $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge1.963$. - Test, observed value: the slope is $0.649$ with standard error $0.0111$, so $t_{obs} \approx 58.6$. - Test, conclusion: since $58.6\ge1.963$, reject a zero slope at the 5% level. The p-value, far below 0.001, gives the same decision. - Interval, formula: $\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,\,872}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$. - Interval, given values: $\hat\beta_1=0.6487$, $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01107$, $t_{0.975,\,872}=1.963$. One more digit than usual avoids rounding error. - Interval, calculations: $0.6487 \pm 1.963 \times 0.01107 = 0.6487 \pm 0.0217$. - Interval: $(0.627,\; 0.670)$, in \$ million agreed per \$ million claimed. - Interval, comparison with the output: the interval by hand matches the interval in the output. - Robust standard errors, yes or no, and why: no. Robust standard errors address the heteroskedasticity only. They do not help with influential observations, with the selection of pitches that ended in a deal, or with a relationship that is not linear. ::: ### Task 5: R² and F (Lecture 3) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the Task 1 model of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation. 1. Calculate SST, SSE, SSR, and $R^2$ from the observed and the fitted values. 2. Compare your $R^2$ with the R-squared in the regression output. 3. Show that the overall F statistic equals $t^2$, with $t$ the t statistic of the slope. Name the two models that the overall F-test compares. 4. Write one concluding sentence that does not claim more than the data show. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: SST, SSE, and SSR: R-squared by hand: R-squared in the output: F and t squared: The two models that the overall F-test compares: Concluding sentence: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) y <- vals$agreed_m yhat <- fitted(val_model) SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2) SSE <- sum((y - yhat)^2) SSR <- sum((yhat - mean(y))^2) c(SST = SST, SSE = SSE, SSR = SSR) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SST SSE SSR 11926.367 2414.572 9511.795 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(R2_manual = 1 - SSE / SST, R2_summary = summary(val_model)$r.squared, F_summary = unname(summary(val_model)$fstatistic["value"]), t_squared = summary(val_model)$coefficients["claimed_m", "t value"]^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R2_manual R2_summary F_summary t_squared 0.7975434 0.7975434 3435.0952236 3435.0952236 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - SST, SSE, and SSR: in squared \$ millions, $\text{SST}\approx11{,}926$, $\text{SSE}\approx2{,}415$, and $\text{SSR}\approx9{,}512$, so $\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}$. - R-squared by hand: $R^2=1-2{,}415/11{,}926\approx0.798$. - R-squared in the output: 0.798, the same value. - F and t squared: the overall F statistic is about 3435. The t statistic of the slope is about 58.6, and $58.6^2\approx3435$, as it must be in simple regression. - The two models that the overall F-test compares: the complete model and the intercept-only model, which predicts the mean agreed valuation for every deal. - Concluding sentence: among these deals, the claimed valuation explains about 80% of the variation in the agreed valuations, but this is an association in a selected set of deals, partly driven by a few influential deals, and not the effect of changing a claim. ::: ### Task 6: A new question: how much more equity do the sharks take? [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} On Shark Tank, the sharks often pay the amount that the founder asks for but take a larger share of the company than the founder offered. Model this pattern directly. Use the same 874 deals for a share of the company (`vals`). Regress the equity agreed in the deal (`deal_equity_pct`) on the equity that the founder first offered (`equity_offered_pct`), both in percent of the company. Report the coefficients, their 95% confidence intervals, and $R^2$. 1. Interpret the slope and the intercept with units, in one sentence each. 2. A founder offers 10% of the company. Which agreed share does the model give as the fitted value? 3. Compare the $R^2$ with that of the valuation model of Task 1 (about 0.798). What does the difference tell a founder? Answer in one or two sentences. 4. Advise the founder in two sentences. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Coefficients with their 95% intervals: R-squared: Interpretation of the slope: Interpretation of the intercept: Fitted agreed share for an offer of 10%: What the difference in R-squared tells a founder: Advice in two sentences: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = vals) summary(equity_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 8.519643 0.73993946 11.51397 1.173912e-28 equity_offered_pct 1.207227 0.05053385 23.88948 1.975473e-97 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(equity_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 7.067372 9.971913 equity_offered_pct 1.108045 1.306410 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(equity_model)$r.squared ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3955808 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Coefficients with their 95% intervals: slope about 1.21, with a 95% interval of about 1.11 to 1.31. Intercept about 8.5, with a 95% interval of about 7.1 to 10.0. - R-squared: about 0.40. - Interpretation of the slope: a founder who offers one percentage point more of the company gives up on average about 1.21 percentage points more in the agreed deal. - Interpretation of the intercept: it is the fitted agreed share for an offer of 0%, and no founder offers 0%, so it has no business meaning of its own. - Fitted agreed share for an offer of 10%: $8.52 + 1.21\times10\approx20.6$% of the company, about twice the offer. - What the difference in R-squared tells a founder: the offered share explains about 40% of the variation in the agreed share, against 80% for the valuations, so single deals lie far from the fitted value more often and the fitted share is a rough guide only. - Advice in two sentences: "For an offer of 10%, expect to give up about 20%, and decide before the pitch how large a share you are willing to give up. These numbers describe what founders who agreed a deal on air gave up, not what would happen to you if you offered a different share." ::: ### Task 7: Check the AI (Lectures 1 to 3) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Tom prepares a pitch. He gave the output of the Task 1 model of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation to an AI assistant. Here is the output: ```text Outcome: agreed valuation ($ millions), 874 deals Estimate Std. Error p-value Claimed valuation ($ millions) 0.649 0.011 <0.001 Intercept -0.068 0.068 0.321 R-squared: 0.798 ``` He asked: "How good is this model?" The AI answered: > "Great model. The claimed valuation predicts the agreed valuation > correctly for about 80% of the deals, because $R^2$ is 0.798. A deal with > a claimed valuation that is \$1 million higher has, on average, an agreed > valuation that is about \$0.65 million higher. And the p-value of the > slope is below 0.001, which proves that the assumptions of the model > hold." 1. The AI answer contains exactly two errors. Name each error and explain it in one sentence. 2. Write one correct sentence about the $R^2$ of 0.798. 3. State in one sentence what the small p-value of the slope does show. Then name in one sentence one result from Task 3 that Tom should know before he trusts this p-value. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text First error: Second error: Correct sentence about the R-squared: What the small p-value does show: A result from Task 3 to know before trusting the p-value: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Filled-in structure: - First error: $R^2$ is the share of the variation in the agreed valuations that the fitted values explain, not a share of deals that the model predicts correctly, and only about 2% of the deals lie within \$10,000 of their fitted value. - Second error: a p-value is calculated under the assumptions of the model, so it cannot prove that they hold. - Correct sentence about the R-squared: "Among these 874 deals, the claimed valuation explains about 80% of the variation in the agreed valuations." - What the small p-value does show: it is strong evidence against a slope of zero, if the assumptions of the model hold. - A result from Task 3 to know before trusting the p-value: the residual plot shows a fan shape, so the homoskedasticity assumption fails and the usual standard error and p-value may be wrong. The second sentence of the AI answer is correct. It is the interpretation of the slope from Task 1. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Individual practice [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Do the sharks pay the amount that a founder asks for? Use the 874 deals for a share of the company (`vals`). Regress the amount agreed in the deal on the amount that the founder asked for, both in thousands of dollars. The code below converts both amounts from dollars to thousands of dollars. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vals$ask_1k <- vals$ask_amount_usd / 1000 # amount asked, in $1,000s vals$deal_1k <- vals$deal_amount_usd / 1000 # amount agreed, in $1,000s ``` ::: 1. Make the scatterplot with the fitted line, and describe it in two sentences. 2. Report the fitted equation with units, and interpret the slope in one sentence. 3. Report the standard error of the slope, its t statistic, its p-value, and its 95% confidence interval. Say in one sentence whether a slope of exactly 1 (one dollar agreed per dollar asked) lies inside the interval. 4. Report $R^2$ and the result of the overall F-test. 5. Inspect the residual plot and the normal Q--Q plot, and write a conclusion of about 120 words. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} amount_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ ask_1k, data = vals) summary(amount_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 27.946252 7.30038928 3.82805 1.383943e-04 ask_1k 1.008318 0.01829848 55.10392 2.740561e-286 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(amount_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 13.6178639 42.274640 ask_1k 0.9724036 1.044232 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(r_squared = summary(amount_model)$r.squared, F = unname(summary(amount_model)$fstatistic["value"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r_squared F 0.7768932 3036.4416122 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # deals that paid exactly, more than, and less than the amount asked c(same = sum(vals$deal_1k == vals$ask_1k), more = sum(vals$deal_1k > vals$ask_1k), less = sum(vals$deal_1k < vals$ask_1k)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` same more less 720 138 16 ``` ::: ::: The code fits the model, prints the coefficient table, the 95% intervals, $R^2$ and the overall F statistic, and then counts how many deals paid exactly, more than, or less than the amount asked. 1. Most deals lie on one straight line on which the amount agreed equals the amount asked. A smaller group lies above that line, where the sharks paid more than the founder asked for, in a few cases millions of dollars more. 2. The fitted equation is $\widehat{\text{agreed}}=27.9+1.008\,\text{asked}$, both in \$1,000s. A founder who asks \$1,000 more agrees on average about \$1,008 more. 3. The standard error is about 0.018, $t\approx55.1$, and the p-value is below 0.001. The 95% interval runs from about 0.972 to 1.044, so a slope of exactly 1 lies inside it. 4. $R^2\approx0.777$: the amount asked explains about 78% of the variation in the amount agreed. The overall F-test ($F\approx3036=t^2$) rejects the intercept-only model at the 5% level, as the slope test does. 5. Conclusion: "Among the 874 deals for a share of the company, the sharks paid about one dollar per dollar asked. In 720 deals (82%) they paid exactly the amount asked, in 138 deals more, and in 16 deals less. The residual plot shows a dense row of residuals just below zero, about $-\$29{,}000$, from the deals that paid exactly the ask, and a few very large positive residuals, up to about \$2.8 million. The Q--Q plot rises steeply at the right end, so the residuals are far from normal. The usual standard errors are therefore only a rough guide. The data contain only pitches that ended in a deal on air, so they do not show that asking for more money would bring more money." ::: ### Check your understanding Complete from memory: 1. A residual is ... 2. The slope's standard error estimates ... 3. A fan shape in the residual plot challenges ... 4. $R^2$ is the proportion of ... 5. In simple regression, the overall F statistic equals ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. The observed outcome minus the fitted value, $e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i$. 2. How much the estimated slope would vary from sample to sample, under the model assumptions. 3. Homoskedasticity, and with it the usual standard errors. 4. The variation of the outcome in the sample that the fitted values explain, $\text{SSR}/\text{SST}$. 5. The squared slope t statistic, $F=t^2$. ::: ### Make it yours :::: {.utility-prompt} Two sentences about your own venture Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Imagine the one simple regression you would show an investor (revenue on customers, orders on advertising spending). Write two sentences. First, name the number from this tutorial that you would put in the headline (slope, interval, or $R^2$), and say why. Second, name the limit from Task 3 or Task 5 that you would state openly next to that number. There is no wrong answer. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student venture that sells boxes of prepared meals on campus. "Headline: the slope with its 95% interval. Each extra €100 of advertising is associated with about 12 to 19 more orders. An investor wants to know how many orders the money brings, and the interval shows how uncertain the number is. Limit: the fan shape in my residual plot shows that orders vary more in busy weeks. So the interval depends on an assumption that my own residual plot puts in doubt." ::: You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant: paste your two sentences and ask it to act as an investor who doubts your numbers. :::: ### More practice For extra exercises on the lectures of this tutorial, with worked solutions, ask Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant. For example: "Give me an extra exercise for Intermediate Tutorial 1. Show the solution only after I send my answer." [Continue to Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do](i04-multiple-regression.qmd). :::
